newsitem.title: FRANCE: French 1997 deficit will exceed three pct - minister.
newsitem.headline: French 1997 deficit will exceed three pct - minister.

text.p: Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Thursday that France's public deficit in 1997, the crucial measurement year for European monetary union, would be more than three percent of gross domestic product.
But he stressed Paris was committed to joining a single European currency on time and vowed that the new Socialist-led government had no intention of letting the deficit run out of control.

Strauss-Kahn's statement to a business conference was the first time a senior minister had stated clearly that France will not meet the strictest reading of the Maastricht treaty budget criterion for joining the single currency.

"What I can see as clearly as everyone is that we are not at the three percent set out in the Finance Act. When you say you are not at three percent, that also means you are not at 3.1 percent either, but I cannot tell you how far we are beyond that," the minister said.
"I have no intention, and nor does the prime minister, of allowing any deficit to run out of control," he said.

Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has said France's finances are in a serious state and ordered an independent audit to report on July 21. His spokesman said earlier the three percent deficit target was not explicitly included in spending guidelines sent to ministers for drawing up the 1998 budget and the Maastricht criterion should be interpreted "as a trend".

Strauss-Kahn also told the Forum de l'Expansion conference: "The government does indeed intend to put France in a position to be able to meet its international commitments concerning the single currency at the planned date."

The Socialist party argued in last month's election campaign that the treaty gives room for a political interpretation of the deficit limit as a trend, and promised not to impose a further bout of austerity to join the euro.
